This article covers what to do in the days immediately following, what wind can do to a roof, and how to decide whether the roof needs attention. What Strong Wind Can Do to a Roof Wind does not usually remove a roof in one piece. More often it works at the edges. Gusts can catch the lower edge of a shingle, flex it upward repeatedly over the course of a storm, and break the sealant bond that holds each course against the one below it. The shingle can settle back into place looking essentially normal while no longer being sealed as it was designed to be. Wind ratings vary by shingle product, manufacturer, installation method, roof condition and whether the shingles were properly sealed in the first place, so there is no single wind speed at which a roof can be said to fail. What can be said generally is that an older roof, or one that has already absorbed several severe weather events, may respond differently than a newer one in sound condition. Several things commonly show up after a wind event: Broken sealant bonds. Often the most consequential and the least visible. A shingle that is no longer sealed may lift more easily in the next storm.Displaced or missing shingles. Usually concentrated on the elevation that faced the wind, and along edges, rakes and ridges.Granule loss. Wind-driven rain and debris can scour the mineral surface that shields the asphalt beneath.Lifted flashing, drip edge and ridge caps. Edges and transitions take the most stress and are often where water finds a way in.Damage from debris. Limbs and airborne material can bruise or puncture the surface in ways that are easy to miss from ground level. The same gusts can also pull gutters away from fascia and stress siding on the windward wall, so it is worth walking the full exterior rather than only looking up. If anything you find gives you pause, an assessment from an established roofing contractor in Columbus, OH is a reasonable next step. The First 72 Hours: A Practical Sequence There is no need to rush into decisions, but there is value in doing a few things while the event is recent. 1. Stay off the roofStorm-damaged and wet roofing can be extremely slippery, and decking weakened by moisture is not always obvious from above. Document what you can seePhotograph each elevation of the house wide enough to show the full roof plane, then take closer shots of anything that looks wrong. Include the yard, the gutters, any debris, and the interior if you find staining. Your phone records the date automatically, and keeping the original files rather than edited copies preserves that information. 3. Check the attic on a dry dayA flashlight in the attic can reveal a great deal: water staining on the underside of the decking, damp or matted insulation, or daylight visible through the roof deck. These may indicate that moisture is reaching places it should not, and they are worth reporting to whoever inspects the roof. 4. Address anything actively letting water inIf there is an obvious opening, covering it is generally appropriate. Many policies ask the policyholder to take reasonable steps to prevent further damage after a loss. Keep receipts for tarps or materials, and keep any damaged materials until the matter is resolved. 5. Arrange a professional assessmentA documented inspection can help you understand the condition of the roofing system and decide on appropriate next steps. It is also the point at which conditions that are invisible from the ground, like broken sealant bonds, are typically identified. Frequently Asked Questions
How often should I have my roof inspected?
Most roofing professionals recommend scheduling a roof inspection at least once every year and after major storms. Regular inspections can identify small issues before they become expensive repairs.
Can missing shingles cause leaks?
Yes. Missing shingles expose the underlying roofing materials to moisture and can allow water to enter the home, eventually leading to leaks and structural damage.
How quickly should roof damage be repaired?
Roof damage should be addressed as soon as possible. Delaying repairs often allows problems to worsen and increases repair costs.
Does hail damage always require roof replacement?
Not necessarily. Some hail damage can be repaired, while severe hail damage may require partial or complete roof replacement. A professional inspection can determine the appropriate solution.
